name: Organic Architecture
summary: A building grows from its site like a plant. Wright, Aalto and Goff set the plan, the structure and the material in one flowing whole that opens to the land, with no fixed façade or box.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building should grow from its site and its use as a living form: the whole and the parts belong together, and the plan flows with the land.
design_principles: Fit the building to the site: set the floor levels to the slope and let rocks, trees and water keep their place.
Plan as a continuous flow with few doors, and open each room to 2 or more sides of the landscape.
Use the cantilever, the curve and the spiral, in spans of 3 to 6m, to make the structure and the form one thing.
Use few materials, 3 or 4, left in their natural state, and run them from the inside to the outside.
Compress the entry to 2.0 to 2.3m, then release it into a space of 3.5 to 5m.
Design the built-in furniture, the light and the garden as parts of the same form.
anti_patterns: A closed box set on a levelled site
A rigid orthogonal grid that ignores the site
Glossy synthetic surfaces and painted-over materials
Rooms cut off by corridors and doors
A building that dominates the landscape

massing.form: Interlocking horizontal and curved volumes that step down the site and reach out in terraces and cantilevers.
massing.proportion: Low and wide: 3 to 6 times longer than high, with the main living room open to the view.
massing.roof: Flat or gently sloping roof planes with deep cantilevers of 2 to 5m, or a roof that follows the hill.
massing.relation_to_ground: Anchored to the ground: a rock outcrop, a stone chimney or a terrace ties the house to the land.

structure.system: Masonry, reinforced concrete and timber; cantilevered slabs and stone piers tie the house to the site.
structure.span_and_module: Cantilevers of 3 to 6m; a planning grid of 1.0 to 1.2m; slab depth of 0.15 to 0.25m.
structure.expression: The cantilever, the stone pier and the curve of the plan state the structure and the form together.

materials.finish: Natural and unpainted: rough stone, board-formed concrete and stained timber, left to age.

facade.composition: A layered front of terraces, parapets and glass: horizontal slabs and stone piers, with no single flat wall.
facade.openings: Corner windows, glass walls and clerestories; the window-to-wall ratio is 30 to 60%.

light_and_space.daylight: Light enters from several sides, low under the eaves and high through clerestories, and the garden extends into the room.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A compressed entry gives way to a flowing living space, with a hearth or a water view as the end of the sequence.
light_and_space.interior_character: A free plan with a ceiling of 2.4 to 3.6m, built-in seats and shelves, a stone hearth and natural materials.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is structural and natural: the grain, the stone course and the patterned block carry it, and no applied motif.

rules.rule: Compress the entry, then release it into a flowing living space.
Extend the cantilevered slabs and terraces along the line of the slope.
Open each main room to a view on 2 or more sides.
Merge living, dining and hearth into one space, with the services at the edge.
Use 3 or 4 materials in every part of the building.
Hold terraces and courts open between the volumes.

emotion.target_response: Harmony and calm: the viewer feels part of the land and sheltered in a flowing home.

avoid_when: The site is flat and urban and the brief asks for a tall repeating block.
The brief asks for a strict modular grid.

modifiers.how: Pull the plan back to horizontal bands under a deep eave, in brick, with a central hearth.
Straighten the plan into a regular grid, white render and ribbon glass.

canonical_works.work: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York

sources.title: Frank Lloyd Wright, An Organic Architecture (Lund Humphries, 1939)
